title: Hello and how are you
goal: Greet someone and answer “how are you?”
tip: Gulf adds -ak when talking to a man and -ich to a woman: shlōnak? / shlōnich? (how are you?).
dialogue: And upon you peace. Hi there!
zēn, il-ḥamdu lillāh. w inta shlōnak?
Good, thank God. And how are you?
items: UAE also: shḥālak? (شحالك); to a woman shḥālich?

title: Sorry and goodbye
goal: Greet by time of day, apologise and say goodbye
tip: Goodbye comes in a pair: one side says fī amān illāh or maʿa s-salāma, and the usual reply to fī amān illāh is fī amān il-karīm. A man says āsif (sorry), a woman āsfa; maʿlēsh works for anyone.
dialogue: الحمد لله. معليش، ما أتكلم عربي زين
il-ḥamdu lillāh. maʿlēsh, ma atkallam ʿarabi zēn
Fine, thank God. Sorry, I don't speak Arabic well.
مشكور. لازم أروح الحين، في أمان الله
mashkūr. lāzim arūḥ il-ḥīn, fī amān illāh
Thanks. I have to go now. Goodbye.

title: Survival words
goal: Ask for things politely and handle not understanding
tip: ī (إي) is the everyday Gulf “yes”. naʿam is a more polite yes, and naʿam? on its own means “pardon?”.
dialogue: Excuse me, do you have water?
items: here you go / go ahead (to a man)
to ask someone to slow down: shwayy shwayy ʿalay (go easy on me)
to a woman: ʿīdi; more polite: mumkin tʿīd? (could you repeat?)

title: Polite requests
goal: Ask for things, find the toilet and thank someone for a favour
tip: mā gaṣṣart (you didn't fall short) is the warm Gulf thank-you for a favour; the reply is mā sawwēna shay (we didn't do anything). allāh ykhallīk softens any request like “please”.
dialogue: Could I have some water, please?
items: thank you, you've been very kind (to a man)
to a woman: mā gaṣṣarti; reply: mā sawwēna shay
excuse me (to pass or leave, to a man)
you have / do you have? (to a man)
shu yaʿni gahwa? = what does gahwa mean?

title: About me
goal: Say your name, where you're from and what you do
tip: There's no word for “am / is / are” in the present: ana ṭālib = I (am a) student.
dialogue: My name is Salim. And you?
I'm Khalid. Where are you from?
I'm from Britain, I study here.
items: to a woman: shismich?; Saudi: wish ismak?
reply: ish-sharaf li (the honour is mine)

title: Work and study
goal: Say whether you work or study, and where
tip: Add fi for “in” or “at”: fi sharika (at a company), fi Dbayy (in Dubai). A woman student is ṭālba; for a woman, verbs to “you” end in -īn: wēn tishtaghlīn?
dialogue: Nice to meet you. Are you a student?
The honour is mine. Yes, and I work.
fi sharika fi Dbayy. w inta?
At a company in Dubai. And you?
I'm a student at the university.
items: where do you work? (to a man)
the honour is mine (reply to tsharrafna)

title: Questions and directions
goal: Ask the five big questions and follow simple directions
tip: Question words can go first or stay where the answer would be: wēn il-masjid? and il-masjid wēn? are both normal. There's no extra word like “do”, and the rest of the sentence keeps statement order.
items: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar: shinu?; Saudi: wish / ēsh?

title: Can and know
goal: Say what you can and can't do, and what you know
tip: ma before a verb makes it negative: agdar (I can) → ma agdar (I can't). ma also goes before ʿind-: ma ʿindi (I don't have). Before other words, use mub (Kuwait: mū): mub zēn, not good.
dialogue: A little. I want to learn Gulf Arabic.
إي أقدر، بس ما أعرف وايد
ī agdar, bas ma aʿarf wāyid
Yes I can, but I don't know much.
items: also very common: ma adri (ما أدري)

title: There is, there isn't, and not
goal: Say what there is and isn't, and say “not” before any word
tip: ma goes before verbs and ʿind- (ma aʿarf, I don't know; ma ʿindi, I don't have). Before other words use mub: mub bārid (not cold), mub hni (not here). Kuwaitis say mū. “There is” is fī and “there isn't” is ma fī (Kuwait: aku / māku).
dialogue: لا، ما في. بس في عصير
la, ma fī. bas fī ʿaṣīr
No, there isn't. But there's juice.
items: not (before anything that isn't a verb)

title: Numbers and prices
goal: Count to five and ask how much
tip: Number + noun: 3 to 10 take a plural (khams dagāyig, five minutes), 11 and up take a singular (ʿishrīn dirham). b- in front of a price means “for”: b-ʿishrīn, for twenty.
items: before a noun: thalāth (thalāth sanawāt, three years)
before a noun: khams (khams dagāyig, five minutes)
Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, Qatar; Saudis say marra or kthīr

title: More numbers
goal: Count to ten, then twenty and a hundred
tip: Arabic digits go left to right like English ones: ٢٥ is 25.
dialogue: And how many brothers do you have?

title: Prices in the souq
goal: Understand prices up to a thousand and bargain once
tip: 11 and up take a singular noun: miya w khamsīn dirham. For exactly two, add -ēn to the noun instead of using thnēn: dirhamēn (two dirhams), sāʿtēn (two hours).
dialogue: la, ākhir siʿir miya w ʿishrīn
No, final price a hundred and twenty.
items: final price / what's your best price?
is-sāʿa cham? = what time is it?

title: At the café
goal: Order food and drink and ask for the bill
tip: abi (I want) comes from the older abghi; you'll hear abgha in western Saudi (Hijaz). To a woman: tabīn? (do you want?). In the UAE you'll often hear abā / tabā (أبا / تبا).
dialogue: abi gahwa w māy law samaḥt
I'd like coffee and water, please.
لا، بس قهوة. والحساب لو سمحت
la, bas gahwa. w il-ḥsāb law samaḥt
No, just coffee. And the bill, please.
items: served with Arabic coffee (gahwa), which has no milk

title: Time and plans
goal: Talk about now, today and tomorrow
tip: Put b- in front of a verb for “will”: arūḥ (I go) becomes barūḥ (I'll go).
dialogue: I'm going to the market now.
أنا بروح باكر إن شاء الله
ana barūḥ bāchir in shāʼ allāh

title: Taxi and the time
goal: Tell a driver where to go, when to turn and where to stop, and ask the time
tip: Commands to a man have no ending (liff, waggif); to a woman add -i (liffi, waggfi). Ask the time with is-sāʿa cham? and answer with is-sāʿa + number: is-sāʿa thalāth (it's three).
dialogue: Hi, where do you want to go?
المول لو سمحت. الساعة كم الحين؟
il-mōl law samaḥt. is-sāʿa cham il-ḥīn?
The mall, please. What time is it now?
It's three, and the mall is close.
items: you already know it from shlōnak
to a woman: liffi; liff yamīn = turn right

title: Visiting and good manners
goal: Use the call-and-response phrases of Gulf hospitality
tip: These come in pairs: learn the reply with the phrase. yaʿṭīk il-ʿāfya → allāh yʿāfīk.
dialogue: الله يحييك. ما شاء الله، البيت وايد حلو
allāh yḥayyīk. mā shāʼ allāh, il-bēt wāyid ḥilu
God bless you. Wow, the house is really nice.
items: thanks for your effort / well done
said to someone working or helping; to a woman: yaʿṭīch il-ʿāfya
